title: Module 1 R Tools
text:
Visualization
Suppose we want to look at how life expectancy in Japan has changed over time using a simple line plot. The ggplot2 package within tidyverse is the best for customizability. It works off the grammar of graphics, the idea that every plot contains layers. You start with data and then map certain variables in your dataset to attributes called aesthetics. After, you can add scales, geometry and other characteristic changes. For a lineplot, there are two aesthetics (an x- and a y- variable) and a simple line geometry.

japan2 |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp))+
  geom_line()








Notice that we first passed the dataset to ggplot using a pipe, defined the aesthetics and then added the geometry (lines in this case). One could also add points as follows

japan2 |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()








Axes labels and titles are added with the labs command

japan2 |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x="Year",y="Life Expectancy",
       title="Life Expectancy vs Time (Japan)")








You can also change colors and background; see Data Carpentry for additional details. The textbook R Cookbook also has great examples.
Two other aesthetics commonly used in graphs are color and size. For example, suppose we wanted to incorporate population and gdp into the above graph.

japan2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp,col=gdpPercap,size=pop))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x="Year",y="Life Expectancy",
       title="Life Expectancy vs Time (Japan)")








This default color palette isn’t great and there are many ways to change it. This also gives us an excuse to talk about the scale layer. You can apply scale to any of your aesthetics in order to change their attributes. Here is an example of how to change color with the popular viridis package:

library("viridis") 
japan2 |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp,col=gdpPercap,size=pop))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x="Year",y="Life Expectancy",
       title="Life Expectancy vs Time (Japan)")+
  scale_color_viridis(name="GDP (per Capita)",option = "A")








Using diverging color schemes (like going from blue to red) is also a popular choice:

japan2 |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp,col=gdpPercap,size=pop))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x="Year",y="Life Expectancy",
       title="Life Expectancy vs Time (Japan)")+
  scale_color_distiller(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1)








The Wes Anderson Palettes are fun too although they require using color gradients instead:

library(wesanderson) 
pal <- wes_palette("Darjeeling1", 100, type = "continuous")
japan2 |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp,col=gdpPercap,size=pop))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x="Year",y="Life Expectancy",
       title="Life Expectancy vs Time (Japan)")+
  scale_color_gradientn(colours=pal)








There are too many options to get into them all but the site Top R Color Palettes has a pretty good list for those who like wasting time messing around with such things (I can relate).

title: Module 1 R Tools
text:
Discrete vs Continuous Aesthetics
In the above example, all of the aesthetics used were continuous variables. Suppose we want to compare Year vs Life Expectancy for the United States vs Japan. Then we would need to include the the discrete variable country as an aesthetic. First, let’s create a new dataset that has only those two the US and Japan. The droplevels command drops all unused values of country (since we are only selecting US and Japan - try running the commands without this line to see the difference).

us_v_japan=gapminder |> 
  filter(country %in% c("Japan","United States")) |>
  select(c('country','year','lifeExp')) |>
  droplevels()
table(us_v_japan$country)


        Japan United States 
           12            12 


Now we can create a scatterplot colored by country. You can use the viridis color schemes or you can manually define the values by name or hex code (the one below gives Pacific orange):

us_v_japan |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp,col=country))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line()+
  labs(x="Year",y="Life Expectancy",
       title="Life Expectancy vs Time")+
  scale_color_manual(values=c("black","#E35205"), name="Country")








One of my favorite discrete color schemes is the following colorblind friendly palette taken from this site:

cb_palette <- c(
  "#000000",  # black
  "#E69F00",  # orange
  "#56B4E9",  # sky blue
  "#009E73",  # bluish green
  "#F0E442",  # yellow
  "#0072B2",  # blue
  "#D55E00",  # vermillion
  "#CC79A7"   # reddish purple
)

Once defined, you can select colors by index:

us_v_japan |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp,col=country))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line()+
  labs(x="Year",y="Life Expectancy",
       title="Life Expectancy vs Time")+
  scale_color_manual(values=cb_palette[c(2,4)], name="Country")








You can also create separate plots for values of a discrete variable using facets.

us_v_japan %>% ggplot(aes(x=year,y=lifeExp))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line()+
  labs(x="Year",y="Life Expectancy",title="Life Expectancy vs Time")+
  facet_wrap(~country)

title: Module 1 R Tools
text:
Histograms and Boxplots
We’ll conclude with two additional visualizations that you will find helpful as we progress through the course.
First, histograms. This is a useful tool for displaying the overall distribution of a single numeric variable like life expectancy:

japan2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x=lifeExp))+
  geom_histogram(fill=cb_palette[4],
                 col="black",
                 breaks=seq(60,85,5))+
  theme_bw()+
  labs(x="Life Expectancy",y="Year")








Note the use of the breaks command to manually define where the bins start and end. Choosing the appropriate bins is one of the most challenging parts of creating a good histogram as you want to balance bias (too few bins will oversmooth the distribution) with variance (too many bins will make the distribution look too jagged). In this case, the shape of the distribution is fairly robust since doubling the number of bins leads to roughly the same unimodal, left skewed shape:

japan2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x=lifeExp))+
  geom_histogram(fill=cb_palette[4],
                 col="black",
                 breaks=seq(60,85,2.5))+
  theme_bw()+
  labs(x="Life Expectancy",y="Year")








You can google Sturges’ Rule to find out more about R’s default choice (which I think rarely looks good).
The second visualization to mention is boxplots. This is a useful tool for comparing the distribution of a numeric variable between two different groups (like US vs Japan):

us_v_japan |>

title: Module 1.3: Inference for SLM
text:
In the last couple of notes, we have gone around slapping trendlines onto data and using them to make predictions. We have some metrics which will help us judge between competing models, but sometimes we might see a linear trend even when none exists. For example, I could randomly generate 30 points and get a line with negative slope.

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(44)
data.frame(x=rnorm(30),y=rnorm(30)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x,y=y))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")








The slope is pretty close to 0 which is what it theoretically should be since our model for generating the data above was just
\[Y_i = 0 \times X_i + \varepsilon_i\]
where \(\varepsilon\_i\) is standard normal, but it is still negative and if we didn’t know it was fake data, we might be tempted to conclude that there is a linear dependence between the variables \(x\) and \(y\) even though there really isn’t.
The inferential approach to linear models asks the following question: is the slope I got “significantly” nonzero. In statistics, significance implies that some kind of hypothesis test is at play. Without rehashing all of introductory statistics, I want to briefly explore two key terms that we will use throughout the course:

Standard Error (SE)
p-value

We’ll do so in the context of finding the slope in an SLM.

title: Module 1.3: Inference for SLM
text:
In the last couple of notes, we have gone around slapping trendlines onto data and using them to make predictions. We have some metrics which will help us judge between competing models, but sometimes we might see a linear trend even when none exists. For example, I could randomly generate 30 points and get a line with negative slope.

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(44)
data.frame(x=rnorm(30),y=rnorm(30)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x,y=y))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")








The slope is pretty close to 0 which is what it theoretically should be since our model for generating the data above was just
\[Y_i = 0 \times X_i + \varepsilon_i\]
where \(\varepsilon\_i\) is standard normal, but it is still negative and if we didn’t know it was fake data, we might be tempted to conclude that there is a linear dependence between the variables \(x\) and \(y\) even though there really isn’t.
The inferential approach to linear models asks the following question: is the slope I got “significantly” nonzero. In statistics, significance implies that some kind of hypothesis test is at play. Without rehashing all of introductory statistics, I want to briefly explore two key terms that we will use throughout the course:

Standard Error (SE)
p-value

We’ll do so in the context of finding the slope in an SLM.

title: Module 1.3: Inference for SLM
text:
Standard Error and p-value
The first thing to note is that in order to talk about the standard error of an estimator, we need to think of it as a random variable with a distribution of possible values called its sampling distribution. Its standard error is then the standard deviation of the sampling distribution (yeah its a mouthful, I know). For example, if I replicate the experiment above by choosing 30 random x and y values 1000 times and computing the estimated slope for each replicate, I will get a distribution of slopes we would expect for random data:

set.seed(45)
slopes = replicate(1000, {
  x = rnorm(30)
  y = rnorm(30)
  coef(lm(y ~ x))[2]
})
hist(slopes)








This type of experiment, where we repeatedly calculate a statistic from replicate samples (or resamples), is called a Monte Carlo Simulation. In the example, the output estimates the null1 sampling distribution of the estimator \(\hat \beta_1\) (i.e. the distribution of possible slopes we might get if the true slope was 0). Notice that the mean is close to 0:

mean(slopes)

[1] 0.007962432


but we get values as large as

max(abs(slopes))

[1] 0.6262668


in absolute value. An estimate of the standard error is the standard deviation of our simulated slopes.

sd(slopes)

[1] 0.1947679


A good rule of thumb is that most observations of a random variable fall within 2–3 standard deviations of its mean2 Using this guideline, our simulation suggests that slopes of randomly generated pairs (using the specific normal parameters above) should typically fall in the interval(lower, upper) where:

cat("lower = ",mean(slopes) -2*sd(slopes), ",upper = ", mean(slopes) +2*sd(slopes))

lower =  -0.3815734 ,upper =  0.3974982


If a computed slope falls outside this range, it would be considered unusual and may indicate that the true slope is significantly nonzero. For instance, if I generate data with the same noise but introduce an actual slope of 1, the estimated slope will fall outside this range, confirming its significance.

  x = rnorm(30)
  y = x+rnorm(30)
  model = lm(y ~ x)
  coef(model)[2]

        x 
0.9367399 


In this case, we would say that the variable \(x\) is a “significant” predictor of \(y\). Its slope matters.
Since we cannot rely on simulations like this for real data3, classical statistics gives us a formula for the standard error of \(\hat \beta_1\)4: \[SE(\hat \beta_1)= \sigma/\sqrt{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2}\]
where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the noise. This formula is baked into lm as well5 and can be viewed using summary. Let’s look at the output of this function for the trump.vote vs non.white model:

df_url="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/election2016.csv"
election2016=read.csv(df_url)
fit_lm=lm(trump.vote~non.white,data=election2016)
summary(fit_lm)


Call:
lm(formula = trump.vote ~ non.white, data = election2016)

Residuals:
      Min        1Q    Median        3Q       Max 
-0.235205 -0.079041  0.003105  0.072068  0.161777 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  0.58113    0.02862  20.307  < 2e-16 ***
non.white   -0.26546    0.08230  -3.226  0.00227 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.09235 on 48 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1781,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.161 
F-statistic:  10.4 on 1 and 48 DF,  p-value: 0.002265


There’s a lot here and we’ll get to more of it later, but for now look at the Estimate and Std Error columns. The estimate \(-0.2656\) next to non.white is the estimated slope and \(0.08230\) is the corresponding standard error. This means that even though our estimate of the slope is \(-0.2656\), we are only confident in that value being accurate up to 2 or 3 times \(0.08230\). This is often phrased in terms of what we call confidence intervals: a 95% confidence interval is roughly equal to the estimate \(\pm 2\times\)SE6. In our example, the 95% confidence interval would be

cat("CI = (", -0.26546-2*0.08230,",", -0.26546+2*0.08230,")" )

CI = ( -0.43006 , -0.10086 )


The p-value is the probability of obtaining a slope of magnitude as large as the one obtained from our data ASSUMING the data was randomly generated from normal random variables (like our fake data above). For example, in our fake data, only

sum(abs(slopes)>0.5)/1000

[1] 0.008


of all our our slopes are as big as \(0.5\) so the p-value of \(0.5\) would be about \(0.008\). Since this number is small, \(0.5\) would be a “significantly nonzero” slope in this scenario. Visually, the p-value is the relative size of the shaded area to the total area shown below:

hist_data = hist(slopes, plot = FALSE)

plot(hist_data, 
     col = ifelse(abs(hist_data$mids) > 0.5, "steelblue", "lightgray"),
     main = "Null Sampling Distribution of Slope",
     xlab = "Slope",
     border = "white")

text(0.5, max(hist_data$counts) * 0.5, "Area = 0.008", col = "steelblue", cex = 0.9)








On the other hand, if we look at the fraction of slopes greater than \(0.1\) in absolute value, we see that

sum(abs(slopes)>0.1)/1000

[1] 0.608


of all slopes were greater than \(0.1\) so the p-value of \(0.1\) would be \(0.608\) . This number is pretty high (there’s a 60% change of generating a slope this large by chance) so \(0.1\) is not a significantly nonzero slope.
The smaller the p-value, the more surprising it would be to get a slope as extreme as we observed due to chance, providing more evidence of a significant linear relationship. By convention, a p-value below \(0.05\) is considered statistically significant, below \(0.001\) is considered highly significant, and between \(0.05\) and \(0.1\) is considered moderately significant, though these are guidelines rather than hard rules.
Looking back at the output of the model above, the stated p-value for our slope was \(0.0027< 0.05\) so we can say that non.white is a statistically significant predictor of trump.vote (even though we say in the last notes its a bad predictor) and since the slope is negative, states with a higher proportion of non-white residents tended to have lower Trump vote.

title: Module 1.3: Inference for SLM
section: Type I and Type II Errors
text:
Type I and Type II Errors
Its important to remember that when talking about statistical significance, there are two types of error one could make

Concluding that a relationship is significant when it is not
Failing to identify a significant relationship

The first is called a Type I error and the second a Type II error. If we look at our experiment from earlier and use a \(2\times\)SE rule for significance, here is how many Type I errors we would make

sum(abs(slopes)>2*sd(slopes))

[1] 43


That’s an error rate of \(43/1000=0.043\). Using a 2SE rule, the answer will usually be close to \(0.05\). In contrast, if I am testing a situation where the actual slope exists but is small (say 0.1), then I would probably make a Type II error since the estimated slope of

set.seed(44)
x = rnorm(30)
y = 0.1*x+rnorm(30)
model = lm(y ~ x)
coef(model)[2]

          x 
0.005773422 


is within 2SE of 0.

title: Module 1.3: Inference for SLM
section: What are those grey areas that appear in geom_smooth?
text:
What are those grey areas that appear in geom_smooth?
The astute observer will have noticed that geom_smooth plots a gray area around a trendline and perhaps questioned why it is has unequal width depending on where we are at on the \(x\)-axis. For example, looking back at the trump.vote model:

election2016 |> ggplot(aes(x=non.white,y=trump.vote))+
  geom_point() +
  labs(x="Non-white Proportion",y="Trump Vote Proportion")+
  geom_smooth(method="lm")








The grey band shows 95% confidence intervals for the predicted mean of \(Y\) at each value of \(x\). Notice that the band is narrowest in the middle of the data and widens toward the edges. This is not a coincidence! The standard error of a predicted mean \(\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\) depends on how far \(x_i\) is from \(\bar{x}\):
\[SE(\hat{y}_i) = \sigma \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_i - \bar{x})^2}{\sum (x_j - \bar{x})^2}}\]
When \(x_i\) is close to \(\bar{x}\), the second term under the square root is nearly zero and the SE is small. As \(x_i\) moves further from \(\bar{x}\) in either direction, the SE grows, reflecting the fact that we are extrapolating further from where most of our data lives. Intuitively, our estimates of \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) each carry their own uncertainty, and that uncertainty compounds as we move away from the center of the data.
One can get such confidence intervals using the predict function. Here are the first six in our Beerwings model. The “fit” term gives the estimate \(\hat{y}\) for the corresponding \(x\) in our data while “lwr” and “upr” give the endpoints for a 95% confidence interval of our estimate:

head(predict(fit_lm,interval = "confidence"))

        fit       lwr       upr
1 0.4882225 0.4611187 0.5153264
2 0.4696406 0.4376342 0.5016471
3 0.4510588 0.4112776 0.4908399
4 0.5121135 0.4846125 0.5396145
5 0.4192041 0.3629583 0.4754500
6 0.4988407 0.4725825 0.5250990


There is a further level of complexity that I hesitate to mention, but we have already gotten deep into the rabbit hole so here we go. There are also something called prediction intervals:

head(predict(fit_lm,interval = "prediction"))

        fit       lwr       upr
1 0.4882225 0.3005821 0.6758629
2 0.4696406 0.2812296 0.6580517
3 0.4510588 0.2611724 0.6409451
4 0.5121135 0.3244153 0.6998117
5 0.4192041 0.2251993 0.6132090
6 0.4988407 0.3113206 0.6863608


The prediction intervals try to take into account the variance of the noise as well and as such, they are always wider than the confidence intervals. Here is a comparison of the interpretations of confidence vs prediction intervals for the first observation in our dataset (Alabama) which had a non-white proportion of

election2016$non.white[1]

[1] 0.35



(Confidence Interval) Based on our model, we are 95% confident that the mean Trump vote of all states with a non-white proportion of 0.35 will be between 0.4611187 and 0.5153264.
(Prediction Interval) Based on our model, we predict with 95% confidence that a randomly selected state with a non-white proportion of 0.35 will have a Trump vote between 0.3005821 and 0.6758629.

To summarize the difference:

Confidence interval for the mean at \(x_i\): how uncertain are we about the average value of \(Y\) at this \(x_i\)? This only accounts for uncertainty in estimating the line.
Prediction interval at \(x_i\): how uncertain are we about a single new observation \(Y\) at this \(x_i\)? This accounts for uncertainty in estimating the line *plus* the irreducible noise \(\sigma\) of any individual observation.

title: Module 1.1: Introduction to Statistical Models
text:
A deterministic model for prediction is a function \[
Y = f(X_1,X_2,..X_p)
\] where \(Y\) is called the outcome or response variable, \(X_1,...,X_p\) are called the features or predictors, and \(f\) is a function which relates the two. A statistical or probabilistic model allows us to add some random noise into the model and say \[
Y = f(X_1,X_2,..X_p) + \varepsilon
\] where \(\varepsilon\) is a random variable with mean zero (so the noise acts in an unbiased manner) and nonzero variance \(\sigma\). In this framework, the function \(f\) represents the trend and the error term \(\varepsilon\) represents random fluctuations in the outcome that are not captured by your features. Because of Central Limit Theorem arguments, we often assume that \(\varepsilon\) is a Normal random variable.
To demonstrate, here is an example of data that is generated according to the statistical model \[
Y = X + Z
\] where \(Z\) is a standard normal random variable and \(X\) can be either 0, 1, or 2:

set.seed(45) # Sets random number generator seed for reproducibility. 
X=rep(c(0,1,2),300) # Generates 300 copies of the list 0,1,2
n=length(X)  # Could set n = 900 but this is better in case we change X
Y=X+rnorm(n) # Adds random noise
plot(X,Y)   # R basic plotting function








Notice that for each possible value of \(X=x\), the corresponding \(Y\) values are normally distributed around \(x\). For example, here are all \(Y\) values corresponding to \(X=0\).

hist(Y[X==0],main="Histogram of Y values for X=0",xlab="Y")








This is what we call fake data. We started with a mathematical model and used it to create observations. Its cheating, but sometimes necessary to pull back the mathematical curtain and get some intuition. In the real world, the opposite happens: we get data and need to guess the model. Assuming we have a single feature \(X\) and outcome \(Y\), then data means collecting \(n\) pairs of points \((x_i,y_i)\), \(i=1,2...,n\), where each \(x_i\) is a measurement of the feature and \(y_i\) is a corresponding measurement on the outcome. In our fake data, this would be all 900 pairs of X,Y values. For example, the first is

c(X[1],Y[1])

[1] 0.0000000 0.3407997


The goal is then to find a predicted trend function \(\hat{f}\) (yes, we like to put hats on things in statistics and it always means something that is predicted) so that the predicted values \[
\hat{y}_i = \hat{f}(x_i)
\] are as close to the collected \(y_i\) as possible. If the outcome variable \(y_i\) is numeric, we call the process of finding a suitable \(\hat{f}\) a regression problem. If the outcome \(y_i\) is categorical, we call it a classification problem. It is also often of interest to find an estimate \(\hat{\sigma}\) for the standard deviation of the noise so we can form confidence or prediction intervals but more on that to come.
Suppose now that we did not know the original model that had been used to generate the \(X\) and \(Y\) values above. How would we go about developing a model of the form \[
Y = f(X) + \varepsilon ?
\] Well, since we assumed that \(\varepsilon\) has mean zero, the trend function \(f(X)\) should capture how the mean of \(Y\) depends on the values of \(X\). From the scatterplot above, it looks like the mean of Y increases as X increases in a linear fashion so we might guess \[
f(X) \approx m X + b
\]
In fact, we could compute the mean of Y for each value of X as follows1 to estimate \(m,b\):

c(mean(Y[X==0]),mean(Y[X==1]),mean(Y[X==2]))

[1] -0.04163491  1.02615796  1.96376055


Here it looks like the mean of Y is roughly 0 when X is 0 and goes up by about 1 for each increase of 1 in X. This would suggest that for any value of \(X = 0,1,2\), \[
f(X) \approx X.
\] To estimate the standard deviation of the noise, we can also compute the standard deviation for each X value

c(sd(Y[X==0]),sd(Y[X==1]),sd(Y[X==2]))

[1] 1.026344 1.047840 1.023557


They are all pretty close to 1 so we might estimate \(\hat{\sigma} \approx 1\). Of course, we know that this model is accurate because this was fake data.
As mentioned above, once you have an estimate of the model, you can use the trend function to calculate predictions. \[
\hat{y} = \hat{f}(x)
\]
In our fake example, \(\hat{f}(x) = x\) so our predictions would just be \[
\hat{y} = x
\] for \(x=0,1,2\). Notice that these predictions will be far from perfect since the actual \(y_i\) values are randomly distributed around \(x_i\). Instead think of \(\hat{y}\) as capturing the expected value of \(Y\) for a given value of \(X=x\). Here is what it looks like plotted alongside our original data

plot(X,Y)
lines(X,X,col='red')








We’ll close out our Day 1 notes with a real life example to further demonstrate these concepts.

If we wanted to predict the outcome of the election, we have two choices

Try to predict the actual proportion of Trump vote (trump.vote)
Try to predict whether the state was red (for Trump) or blue (for Clinton) (outcome)

The first would be a regression problem and the second classification. We’ll start with the first and choose the single predictor non.white (the proportion of non-white residents of the state) to use in our preliminary analysis.
The most common package we will use in this course is tidyverse. If you haven’t already, install it with the command install.packages('tidyverse'). Then get in the habit of loading it to start each session with the following command.

library(tidyverse)

The tidyverse package contains ggplot2, the premier plotting package2 in R and dare I say any data science software? The following creates a scatterplot of trump.vote vs non.white

ggplot(election2016,
       aes(x=non.white,y=trump.vote))+
  geom_point(shape=1)+
  labs(x="Proportion Non-White Residents",y="Proportion of Trump Vote")+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",se=FALSE,col="darkorange")+
  theme_bw()








The geom_smooth command adds the “trendline” which has a negative slope in this example and seems to capture the overall “flow” of data. This suggests we might fit a model of the form \[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon
\] where \(Y\) = trump.vote, \(X\) = non.white, and \(\varepsilon\) is the random noise. In this case, \[
f(X)= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X
\] is a linear function3 and so estimating it is equivalent to estimating the two parameters \(\beta_0, \beta_1\) with some \(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1\). The predicted outcomes would then be \[
\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i
\] For example, if we look at the line in the graph above, it looks like it has a slope of about \(-0.05/0.2 = -0.25\) and an intercept of around 0.57 so we might guess \[
\hat{\beta}_0 =0.57, \,  \hat{\beta}_1 = -0.25
\] Then the actual and predicted values would be as follows

y=election2016$trump.vote
x=election2016$non.white
yhat=0.57-0.25*x

The Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) of a model is (as it sounds) the sum of squared errors made by replacing the outcome values \(y_i\) with their predictions \[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i- \hat{y}_i)^2
\] We can compute SSE for our model as follows

sse=sum((y-yhat)^2)
cat("SSE = ", sse)

SSE =  0.4116437


If someone chooses a different \(\hat{f}\) that gives predictions with a better SSE, they can claim a better model. But wait a minute, instead of just guessing, can’t we start with our goal of minimizing SSE and find the coefficients which make it as small as possible? In other words, we should think of the SSE as a function of \(\beta_0, \beta_1\) (different lines gives a different error) and try to minimize the “loss” function4): \[
\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1) = SSE = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i))^2
\]
Minimize means choosing estimates \(\hat{\beta}_0,\hat{\beta}_1\) to make this quantity as small as possible. This becomes a calculus or linear algebra problem5 and solving it gives the least squares estimates of \(\beta_0, \beta_1\). The R function lm will compute them by

lm(y~x)


Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x  
     0.5811      -0.2655  


The number under “Intercept” is the estimate \(\hat \beta_0\) and the number under \(x\) is \(\hat \beta_1\).
Before we show this is better than our eyeball model, a note on R syntax. The part of the above command \[
y \sim x
\]
is called a model formula. It means that we are going to be using the variable y as our outcome and variable x as a feature. If you place a function \(f\) around a model formula, then what you are doing is fitting a model \[
Y = f(X) + \varepsilon
\] based on our data. The “lm” stands for linear model which means \(f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) is the trend function being used in this example, but we will replace lm with more complicated functions as the course goes on.
Now let’s check that our model is better than the eyeball one

yhat_lm=0.5811-0.2655*x
sse_lm=sum((y-yhat_lm)^2)
cat("SSE eyeball =",sse," Best SSE = ", sse_lm)

SSE eyeball = 0.4116437  Best SSE =  0.409327


Just a little bit smaller!

title: Module 1.1: Introduction to Statistical Models
text:
Assessing Model Fit
The mathematician George Box once said that “all models are wrong, some models are useful.” The goal of statistical modeling is not a perfect description of real world phenomena but rather a helpful approximation that is “good enough” for the purpose at hand. Once we have fit a model \(\hat y = \hat f (x)\) to a dataset, there are two types of questions we want to ask:

Does the model yield accurate predictions for new observations?
Does the model allow us to infer generalizable relationships between variables?

These two types of questions fall under the categories of prediction and inference, respectively. The latter is the classical domain of mathematical statistics and probably what you are more familiar with if you’ve taken an introduction to statistics course (confidence intervals and hypothesis testing fall under this category). The former is of more concern in the age of machine learning where we often don’t care as much about how our model makes predictions (although maybe we should) so much as the strength of such predictions. The next two sections will delve more into each topic with respect to the linear model considered in this section. If you want to dig even deeper, the Module 1 Theory supplement covers the mathematics behind least squares estimation (calculus background recommended), and the Module 1 R Tools supplement is a helpful primer if you are new to R or ggplot2.

title: Course page for Math 133: Statistical Learning Methods
text:
Close your eyes and think of a time you tried to predict something. What was it it that you were trying to predict? Was it a number? Was it a binary outcome (like win/lose)? What information did you use to make your prediction?
In this class, prediction will be our goal and we’ll develop a toolbox of methods for predicting one variable (called an outcome or response variable) from others (called features or predictors). We’ll cover two main types of problems: regression (predicting a number, like a grade point average) and classification (predicting a category, like whether or not you pass a class). Along the way, you’ll get hands-on experience building and evaluating a wide range of popular models, from foundational ones like linear and logistic regression to more modern approaches like ensemble methods and neural networks.

title: Course page for Math 133: Statistical Learning Methods
text:
What Will We Cover?
The three primary learning objectives for this course are as follows:

Describe, implement, and compare common predictive models in statistics (Develop Tools)

Linear models, including ordinary least squares and logistic regression
Shrinkage methods, such as Ridge and Lasso regression
K-nearest neighbors regression and classification
Classification and regression trees
Principal Component Analysis
Clustering algorithms
Random forests
Gradient boosted models
Neural networks
Models with serial correlation (eg. Random walks, autoregressive models, moving average models)

Select the most applicable statistical tool given a specified research objective (Select Tools)

Distinguishing between regression and classification problems
Distinguishing between supervised and unsupervised algorithms
Evaluating model performance
Model training and validation
Resampling methods
Variable selection
Hyperparameter tuning
Autocorrelation functions and stationarity

Communicate the results of predictive analyses with verbal, visual, and numerical descriptions

Calculate summary statistics and create tables in R
Interpret model output in R
Create appropriate figures using the ggplot2 package in R
Present results using notebooks style programs (eg. quarto, google collab)


All of this will be done in R, a widely used programming language in statistics and data science, so you’ll leave the course with both the conceptual understanding and the practical coding skills that are valued in industry and graduate school.

title: Course page for Math 133: Statistical Learning Methods
text:
Who Is This Course For?
This course is designed for an audience with some basic background in both coding and statistics, but you don’t need to be an expert in either. Specifically we assume:

Coding: You are familiar with fundamental programming concepts like variables, lists, and functions. Some prior experience with R is helpful but not required.
Statistics: You have some introductory statistics knowledge, such as familiarity with measures of center and spread (eg. mean, standard deviation), the normal distribution, and basic graphical displays (eg. histograms, scatterplots). We won’t be starting from scratch on the statistical side but we also won’t assume anything beyond the basics.

If that sounds like you, you’re in the right place! For students with a little more math background (calculus and linear algebra), we’ve also included some supplementary sections in each module to demonstrate the magical theoretical underpinnings of our algorithms.

title: Module 1.2: Prediction for SLM
text:
Last class, we discussed the concept of a statistical model and introduced our first model in R: a simple linear model
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon
\] where \(\varepsilon\) is a normal random variable with standard deviation \(\sigma\). We shall henceforth call this model a simple linear model (SLM).
We introduced the function lm to estimate coefficients in an SLM from a given set of observations and used it to start exploring the relationship between trump.vote and non.white in the election2016 dataset:

library(tidyverse)
df_url="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/election2016.csv"
election2016=read.csv(df_url)
y=election2016$trump.vote
x=election2016$non.white
lm(y~x)


Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x  
     0.5811      -0.2655  


The output tells us that the best linear equation for predicting \(y=trump.vote\) from \(x=non.white\) is \(\hat y = 0.5811 - 0.2655x\). For example, if I have a state that is 50% white, than the predicted trump vote (as a proportion) would be

0.5811-0.2655*0.5

[1] 0.44835


The real test of a model then is how well it predicts new data, but that often first involves assessing how it fits the data used to estimate model paramaters in the first place (called the training data). Before we get into that, a couple comments on R.
The most efficient way to use lm and other modeling functions is to pass the formula and data directly as inputs:

lm(trump.vote ~ non.white,data=election2016)


Call:
lm(formula = trump.vote ~ non.white, data = election2016)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)    non.white  
     0.5811      -0.2655  


However, if you want use the model to predict new values it is helpful to first save the output of lm to a variable and then refer to that variable in future calls:

fit_lm=lm(trump.vote ~ non.white,data=election2016)
print(fit_lm)


Call:
lm(formula = trump.vote ~ non.white, data = election2016)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)    non.white  
     0.5811      -0.2655  


One advantage of this approach is that instead of manually calculating the predicted values \(\hat y = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1x\) for new or old observations, we can use the predict function. For example, to predict the Trump vote when the non-white proportion is 0.5, we do

new_df=data.frame(non.white=0.5)
predict(fit_lm,new_df)

        1 
0.4484042 


That may seem more tedious than just using the formula, but it won’t when the formulas get more complicated. The predict function is also helpful becaue we can pass multiple \(x\) values and get all the predictions at once:

new_df=data.frame(non.white=seq(0,1,0.1))
predict(fit_lm,new_df)

        1         2         3         4         5         6         7         8 
0.5811319 0.5545863 0.5280408 0.5014953 0.4749497 0.4484042 0.4218587 0.3953132 
        9        10        11 
0.3687676 0.3422221 0.3156766 


Or if you want to determine the predicted values for all points in the original dataset, leave the second input blank and this is done by default (first six shown below):

yhat_lm=predict(fit_lm)
head(yhat_lm)

        1         2         3         4         5         6 
0.4882225 0.4696406 0.4510588 0.5121135 0.4192041 0.4988407 


This will be useful in the next section!

title: Module 1.2: Prediction for SLM
text:
Prediction Metrics on Training Set
The data we use to fit the model is called the training set. There are numerous metrics we could introduce to measure how well our model fits the training set. We introduced one in the first notes, namely
\[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat y_i)^2
\]
For scaling purposes, it is more common to use the Mean Squared Error (MSE) defined as the average squared error per observation:
\[
MSE = SSE/n
\]
This can be calculated using the predicted outputs as follows

y = election2016$trump.vote
yhat_lm = predict(fit_lm)
mse = mean((y-yhat_lm)^2)
print(mse)

[1] 0.008186537


Unfortunately, the MSE on its own has the meaningless units of \((y\; units)^2\) (variance anyone?) so it is more common to look at its square root, the R(oot)MSE:

rmse <- sqrt(mse)
print(rmse)

[1] 0.09047949


This says that our predictions are off by about 0.09 per state on average, although not exactly, since squaring the errors before taking the square root is not the same as simply averaging the absolute errors which instead leads to the Mean Absolute Deviation (best acronym in statistics: MAD):

mad=mean(abs(y - yhat_lm))
print(mad)

[1] 0.07823563


The difference comes down to how each metric penalizes errors. RMSE squares the errors before averaging, which gives extra weight to large mistakes, while MAD treats all errors equally regardless of size. This is similar to the difference between the \(\ell_2\) and \(\ell_1\) norms if you know about such things (if not, they will appear later in the course). Both are valid ways of measuring model accuracy; RMSE has more theoretical appeal but MAD is much easier to explain to your friends.
The final, and perhaps most commonly used metric for simple linear models, is \(R^2\) (sometimes called the Coefficient of Determination but usually just R-squared). We’ll first give the calculation and then the explanation:

ybar=mean(y)
sst=sum((y-ybar)^2)
sse=sum((y-yhat_lm)^2)
r2=1-sse/sst
print(r2)

[1] 0.178141


\(R^2\) gives the proportion of variance explained by the model. To explain this phrase, SST (Sum of Squares Total) represents the overall variance in \(y\) values. It is the inherent variability in outcomes and the goal is to explain as much of that variance as possible with our models. SSE is the overall error in our model predictions or the variance left after we account for the relationship with our predictor. SSE/SST is therefore the fraction of the overall variance in outcomes that is NOT explained by the model and 1 - SSE/SST is the fraction that IS explained by our model. A perfect model would have an SSE of 0 and hence, an \(R^2\) value of 1. Here is a function you can use to compute the \(R^2\) for a model given an outcome \(y\) and predicted values \(\hat y\):

get_r2=function(y,yhat){
  ybar=mean(y)       
  sst=sum((y-ybar)^2) # total variance in y
  sse=sum((y-yhat)^2) # variance unexplained by model
  r2=1-sse/sst    # proportion of variance explained by model
  r2
}

#Example usage from scratch
y=election2016$trump.vote
fit_lm=lm(trump.vote~non.white,data=election2016)
yhat=predict(fit_lm)
r2=get_r2(y,yhat)
print(r2)

[1] 0.178141


We’ll need this in the next section. You can also get the \(R^2\) value for the training data using the summary function:

sum_lm=summary(fit_lm)
print(sum_lm$r.squared)

[1] 0.178141


Note that \(R^2\) is just another way of looking at SSE/MSE/RMSE. Any one of these four is sufficient when comparing models. The advantage of \(R^2\) is that it is dimensionless so it could be interpreted more universally. Here are some general guidelines for deciding what is “large” (generated with the help of AI, but complemented with my experience in statistical consulting):

Guidelines for Interpreting \(R^2\)

Large (\(R^2 \geq 0.7\)): The model explains a large proportion of variance. Common in fields like physics or engineering where relationships tend to be more deterministic (e.g., natural sciences1 often see \(R^2 > 0.8\)).
Moderate (\(0.3 \leq R^2 < 0.7\)): The model explains a moderate proportion of variance. Frequently seen in fields like economics or other social sciences, where real-world data involve many unobserved factors.
Small (\(R^2 < 0.3\)): The model explains a small proportion of variance, but can still be meaningful. In fields like psychology, sociology, or behavioral sciences, an \(R^2\) of 0.1–0.2 may actually be considered quite good since human behavior is complex and influenced by many factors.

title: Module 1.2: Prediction for SLM
text:
Training-Testing Validation
Testing set validation means to split off some fraction of your data (usually 20-30%) for testing how well the model predicts “new data”. The observations used for testing are called the hold-out set or sometimes just testing data. Splitting the data into training and testing sets is called partitioning the data. In R, this can be done by deciding on the fraction \(p\) to use for your training set and then sampling \(n*p\) random rows from the dataset as the training set, using the excluded rows for testing:

set.seed(45)
n=nrow(election2016)
p=0.7 # Decide on fraction to keep for training, in this case 70%
train_rows=sample(n,0.7*n) # Choose training rows
train_df=election2016[train_rows,] # Extract training data
test_df= election2016[-train_rows,] # Extract testing data

This would be called a “70-30 split” because we used 70% for training and 30% for testing. We fit our model to the training set

fit_lm_train=lm(trump.vote~non.white,data=train_df)

And calculate any validation metrics like R2 on the testing set

y_test=test_df$trump.vote
yhat_test=predict(fit_lm_train,test_df)
r2_test=get_r2(y_test,yhat_test)
print(r2_test)

[1] -0.2826803


Validation metrics will generally be smaller on the test set BUT less likely to be misleadingly large due to overfitting (more on this topic to come). We can see in this example that \(R^2\) came out negative on the testing set which means that our model did terrible at predicting new data (it would have been better to just guess the mean of \(y\) for all our observations).
Every time we do the training-testing set split we will get a different value for \(R^2\) on the testing set due to the randomness of our partition. For example, running the same code again yields

n=nrow(election2016)
p=0.7 
train_rows=sample(n,0.7*n)  
train_df=election2016[train_rows,] 
test_df= election2016[-train_rows,] 
fit_lm_train=lm(trump.vote~non.white,data=train_df)
y_test=test_df$trump.vote
yhat_test=predict(fit_lm_train,test_df)
r2_test=get_r2(y_test,yhat_test)
print(r2_test)

[1] -0.04216912


Well, the answer was still negative. Overall, this repetition seems to be a sign that despite passing the visual test and (as we’ll see in the next section) the inference test, non.white is not a very good predictor of trump.vote. Later we’ll discuss cross-validation, a method for repeatedly performing training-testing splits in a systematic way. For now, get some practice trying creating these splits.

title: Module 1 Theory: A deeper look into the least squares line
text:
Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm used to minimize a loss function by iteratively adjusting parameters. The idea is that if your desired trend function \(f\) depends on multiple parameters \(\beta_i\), \(i=1,..,p\), then you can look at the partial derivative of the loss function \(\ell = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - f(x_i))^2\) with respect to each parameter. Since the gradient vector, whose \(i\)th component is \[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta_i}
\] always points in the direction of maximum increase, subtracting a small enough multiple of the gradient vector from your current estimates will move towards the minimum of \(\ell\) (which is what we want).
In this tutorial, we’ll use gradient descent to fit a line to data by minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE) for SLM. For convenience, we’ll use \(m,b\) for the slope and intercept. After, we’ll discuss an exact formula for the least squares coefficients as well as a formula for the standard error.

title: Module 1 Theory: A deeper look into the least squares line
text:
Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm used to minimize a loss function by iteratively adjusting parameters. The idea is that if your desired trend function \(f\) depends on multiple parameters \(\beta_i\), \(i=1,..,p\), then you can look at the partial derivative of the loss function \(\ell = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - f(x_i))^2\) with respect to each parameter. Since the gradient vector, whose \(i\)th component is \[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta_i}
\] always points in the direction of maximum increase, subtracting a small enough multiple of the gradient vector from your current estimates will move towards the minimum of \(\ell\) (which is what we want).
In this tutorial, we’ll use gradient descent to fit a line to data by minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE) for SLM. For convenience, we’ll use \(m,b\) for the slope and intercept. After, we’ll discuss an exact formula for the least squares coefficients as well as a formula for the standard error.

title: Module 1 Theory: A deeper look into the least squares line
text:
Problem Setup
Suppose we have collected a dataset of points \((x_i, y_i)\). Our goal is to fit a line \(\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) by minimizing the sum of squared errors:
\[
\ell(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i))^2
\]
We’ll start by generating some fake data:

set.seed(45)
n = 100
x = seq(1, 10, length.out = n)
b1 = 2
b0 = 5
y = b0+b1*x + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 2) # Add noise
data = data.frame(x = x, y = y)

title: Module 1 Theory: A deeper look into the least squares line
text:
Gradient Descent Algorithm
The gradient descent update rules will be:
\[ \beta_i \leftarrow \beta_i - \alpha \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta_i} \] for \(i=1,2\) where \(\alpha\) is a hyperparameter called the learning rate or step size.. The partial derivatives of the loss function can be calculated as:
\[ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta_1} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) \]
\[\frac{\partial \ell }{\partial \beta_0} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) \]
One can implement this in R as follows (epochs is commonly used in machine learning to refer to the number of iterations performed):

gradient_descent = function(x, y, learning_rate = 0.01, epochs = 1000) {
  m = 0 # Initial slope
  b = 0 # Initial intercept
  n = length(y) # Number of data points
  
  for (i in 1:epochs) {
    # Predicted values
    y_pred = m * x + b
    
    # Gradients
    gradient_m = (-2 / n) * sum(x * (y - y_pred))
    gradient_b= (-2 / n) * sum(y - y_pred)
    
    # Update parameters
    m = m - learning_rate * gradient_m
    b = b - learning_rate * gradient_b
  }
  
  return(list(intercept = b, slope = m))
}

# Run gradient descent
gd_result <- gradient_descent(data$x, data$y, learning_rate = 0.01, epochs = 1000)
gd_result

$intercept
[1] 5.009543

$slope
[1] 2.02367


The results should roughly match those obtained by lm:

lm(y~x,data=data)


Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x, data = data)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x  
      5.134        2.005  


We might be able to get closer by adjusting the learning rate or number of epochs

gradient_descent(data$x, data$y, learning_rate = 0.02, epochs = 2000)

$intercept
[1] 5.134328

$slope
[1] 2.005098


But you have to be careful because using a learning rate too high will cause the solutions to diverge.

gradient_descent(data$x, data$y, learning_rate = 0.1, epochs = 1000)

$intercept
[1] NaN

$slope
[1] NaN


And too small will be slower to converge

gradient_descent(data$x, data$y, learning_rate = 0.001, epochs = 1000)

$intercept
[1] 1.843221

$slope
[1] 2.494913


Choosing the right learning rate is a complicated problem. Many modern algorithms use adaptive learning rates (eg. Adam, RMSprop, and AdaGrad) that change to match the size of the gradient (larger gradients need smaller learning rates).

title: Module 1 Theory: A deeper look into the least squares line
text:
Exact Formulas
For SLM, gradient descent is overkill because we can explicitly solve for the least squares solutions by setting the partial derivatives to 0:
\[ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta_1} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)=0 \]
\[\frac{\partial \ell }{\partial \beta_0} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)=0 \]
and solving for \(\beta_0, \beta_1\). Doing so1 yields the explicit formulas
\[\hat \beta_1 = \frac{n \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \sum_{i=1}^n y_i}{n \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right)^2} \]
\[ \hat \beta_0 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i - \hat \beta_1 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{n} \]
that one often sees in stats textbooks. These formulas are used by lm, but you can hard-code them easily enough:

sx=sum(x)
sy=sum(y)
sxx=sum(x^2)
sxy=sum(x*y)
n=nrow(data)

slope= (n*sxy - sx*sy)/(n*sxx-sx^2)
intercept=(sy-slope*sx)/n
cat("slope =", slope, "\n intercept =", intercept)

slope = 2.005098 
 intercept = 5.13433

title: Module 1 Theory: A deeper look into the least squares line
text:
Standard Error
If we substitute \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i\) and \(\bar{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \bar{x}\) into our formula for \(\hat \beta_1\) , we get: \[ \hat{\beta_1} = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(\beta_1(x_i - \bar{x})+\epsilon_i)}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \] which simplifies to \[
\hat{\beta_1} = \beta_1 + \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x}) \epsilon_i}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\] The variance is then: \[
\text{Var}(\hat{\beta_1}) = \text{Var} \left( \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x}) \epsilon_i}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \right)
\] Since the noise terms \(\epsilon_i\) are independent with variance \(\sigma^2\), standard properties of variance imply: \[
\text{Var}\left(\sum (x_i - \bar{x}) \epsilon_i\right) = \sigma^2 \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2
\] Therefore, \[
\text{Var}(\hat{\beta_1}) = \frac{\sigma^2 \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{\left(\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2\right)^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\] The standard error is the square root of this quantity.
The predicted mean of \(Y\) at a given \(x_i\) is: \[
\hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i
\] so by general variance of a sum of random variables formula, the variance of \(\hat{Y}\) is: \[
\text{Var}(\hat{Y}) = \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_0) + x_i^{2} \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) + 2x_i \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1) ]
\] Hmm, now I am realizing this is getting nasty as you have to calculate \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_0)\) and \(\text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1)\). It can be done, but who has time for such algebra in today’s day and age? Hopefully, this at least gives you an idea about why \(x_i\) enters the equation. The textbook Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R covers the details of these calculations. There are also some more general proofs of formulas for multiple regression models that utilize linear algebra and we’ll discuss those in the Module 2 Theory Supplement.

title: Module 2.2: Enriching Linear Models
text:
This section will focus on three additions to the multiple regression models discussed in the last section:

Qualitative predictors
Interaction terms
Polynomial terms

All three topics are examples of feature engineering: building new input variables from existing ones to capture relationships that a raw linear model would miss. Despite these enrichments, the model remains linear in its coefficients, so everything we have learned so far still applies.
We’ll be using three datasets to demonstrate concepts: the Beerwings dataset, the advertising dataset, and the mtcars dataset which is built into R.

title: Module 2.2: Enriching Linear Models
text:
Qualitative Predictors
The Beerwings dataset introduced at the end of Module 1.3 contains information on gender, hotwings and beer consumption for 30 patrons of a Minneapolis bar.

library(tidyverse)
df_url="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/Beerwings.csv"
beerwings=read.csv(df_url) |>
  select(-ID)
head(beerwings)

  Hotwings Beer Gender
1        4   24      F
2        5    0      F
3        5   12      F
4        6   12      F
5        7   12      F
6        7   12      F


In the practice problem, you were asked to fit a SLM
\[
Beer = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times Wings + \varepsilon
\]
We also might want to look at the relationship between Gender and Beer consumption by considering a model of the form
\[
Beer = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times Gender + \varepsilon
\]
as it seems there is definitely a difference in beer consumption between the two groups:

beerwings |>
  ggplot(aes(x=Gender,y=Beer,fill=Gender))+
  geom_boxplot(width=0.5)+
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#0072B2","#D55E00"))+
  theme_classic()








The standard way of incorporating qualitative or categorical variables like Gender into statistical models is via a process called dummy coding1. If the variable is binary2, we choose one value to serve as the baseline for the model (R does this by alphabetical order so it will choose “F” in this example). The baseline value is recoded with a 0, and the other value with 1. In other words, we would define a new variable \[
GenderM = \begin{cases}1 & \text{if  Gender == "Male"} \\ 0 & \text{if  Gender == "Female"} \end{cases}
\]
and then add this as a predictor in our SLM.
Variables constructed in this way are called dummy variables. We can engineer them in R using ifelse:

beerwings$GenderM = ifelse(beerwings$Gender=="M",1,0)
table(beerwings$Gender,beerwings$GenderM)

   
     0  1
  F 15  0
  M  0 15


Then we run lm with the new variable

fit_lm=lm(Beer ~ GenderM,beerwings)
summary(fit_lm)


Call:
lm(formula = Beer ~ GenderM, data = beerwings)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
 -30.4   -6.4    2.0    7.4   17.6 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)   22.000      2.902   7.580 2.95e-08 ***
GenderM        8.400      4.104   2.047   0.0502 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 11.24 on 28 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1301,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.09906 
F-statistic: 4.189 on 1 and 28 DF,  p-value: 0.05019


To interpret this, males (GenderM =1) consumed about 8.4 more wings on average than females (GenderM=0) although the result was only moderately significant3 (p-value = 0.0502)
Engineering a new variable through one-hot encoding was intentionally tedious to illustrate the steps involved. In the future, we’ll just have R do it automatically within the lm call:

lm(Beer ~ Gender,beerwings)


Call:
lm(formula = Beer ~ Gender, data = beerwings)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)      GenderM  
       22.0          8.4  


Notice that it adds “M” at the end of Gender to tell us which value is treated as a “1” in the encoding. You can directly use such calls in the future.
For qualitative predictors with \(k \geq 2\) categories, the idea is similar. We choose one category to serve as baseline and then we create \(k-1\) binary variables for the other categories of the form \[
X_j = \begin{cases}1 & \text{if  Category ==} j \\ 0 & \text{if  Category !=} j\end{cases}
\]
Note that != is R language for “not equal to”. The \(X_j\) are called indicator or (group) dummy variables. Again, lm is built to handle this kind of stuff. Let’s illustrate using the Math 37 survey dataset from the Module 1 Assessment

title: Module 2.2: Enriching Linear Models
text:
Interaction Terms
Returning to our Beerwings example, suppose we want to jointly look at the impact of Gender and Hotwings on Beer consumption:

beerwings |>
  ggplot(aes(x=Hotwings,y=Beer,color=Gender))+
  geom_point(shape=1)+
  scale_color_manual(values=c("#0072B2","#D55E00"))+
  geom_smooth(method=lm,se=F)+
  theme_classic()








There are two separate questions we could ask

Do the two lines have the same intercept?
Do the two lines have the same slope?

The first can be answered by considering a multiple regression model of the form
\[
Beer = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times Gender + \beta_2 \times Hotwings + \varepsilon
\]
The \(\beta_1\) serves as the “shift” in intercept between Gender = 0 (F) and Gender = 1 (M) because if Gender = 0 we get
\[
Beer = \beta_0  + \beta_2 \times Hotwings + \varepsilon
\] and if Gender = 1, we get
\[
Beer = (\beta_0 + \beta_1)  + \beta_2 \times Hotwings + \varepsilon
\]
so \(\beta_1\) is the difference in intercepts. This is just another application of multiple regression

fit_lm=lm(Beer~Gender+Hotwings,beerwings)
summary(fit_lm)


Call:
lm(formula = Beer ~ Gender + Hotwings, data = beerwings)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-16.7854  -5.0496   0.7114   2.7953  18.7114 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   2.5506     3.8125   0.669    0.509    
GenderM      -2.4361     3.3042  -0.737    0.467    
Hotwings      2.0839     0.3512   5.934 2.52e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.541 on 27 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6224,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5945 
F-statistic: 22.26 on 2 and 27 DF,  p-value: 1.946e-06


Note that the coefficient of GenderM was not significant (although interestingly, it was negative!) so we conclude that the intercepts for Male and Female were not significantly different. To test for a difference in slopes, we can add an interaction term and consider the model
\[
Beer = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (Gender) + \beta_2 (Hotwings) + \beta_3 (Gender \times Hotwings)+  \varepsilon
\]
To see why this works, note that if Gender = 0, the model becomes \[
Beer = \beta_0 + \beta_2 (Hotwings)+  \varepsilon
\] while if Gender = 1, we get \[
Beer = \beta_0 + \beta_1 + (\beta_2+\beta_3)  (Hotwings)+  \varepsilon
\]
So \(\beta_3\) is the difference in the slopes and \(\beta_1\) is still the difference in the intercepts.
Adding an interaction term is the same as engineering a new variable whose values are \(Hotwings \times Gender\), but again lm will do this automatically if you include both variables with a * between them:

fit_lm_int=lm(Beer~Gender*Hotwings,beerwings)
summary(fit_lm_int)


Call:
lm(formula = Beer ~ Gender * Hotwings, data = beerwings)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.7632  -4.5789   0.6316   2.7716  18.6316 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        0.3158     5.7089   0.055 0.956310    
GenderM            1.9737     8.9429   0.221 0.827051    
Hotwings           2.3233     0.5740   4.048 0.000413 ***
GenderM:Hotwings  -0.3891     0.7317  -0.532 0.599379    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.643 on 26 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6265,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5834 
F-statistic: 14.54 on 3 and 26 DF,  p-value: 9.304e-06


In this case, the coefficient of GenderM:Hotwings tells us the estimate of \(\beta_3\). In this case it is negative, but insignificant so we conclude that gender does not impact beer consumption after accounting for wings consumption (i.e. if you have two people consume the same number of wings, our model would predict the same beer consumption regardless of gender).
We can also include interactions between numeric predictors like in the advertising dataset. Remember that 3D plot we showed in Module 2.1 and my comment about wanting to peal down the surface? Well we can do that if we consider the model \[
sales = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (TV) + \beta_2 (radio) + \beta_3 (TV \times radio) + \varepsilon
\]
which creates an estimation function of the form \[
\hat y = a + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_1x_2
\]
It turns out the interaction between TV and radio is significant:

df_url="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/Advertising.csv"
advertising=read.csv(df_url)
sales_lm_int=lm(sales~TV*radio,data=advertising)
summary(sales_lm_int)


Call:
lm(formula = sales ~ TV * radio, data = advertising)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-6.3366 -0.4028  0.1831  0.5948  1.5246 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 6.750e+00  2.479e-01  27.233   <2e-16 ***
TV          1.910e-02  1.504e-03  12.699   <2e-16 ***
radio       2.886e-02  8.905e-03   3.241   0.0014 ** 
TV:radio    1.086e-03  5.242e-05  20.727   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.9435 on 196 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9678,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9673 
F-statistic:  1963 on 3 and 196 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Even more rewarding is to re-examine the 3D plot with this new model:

library(plotly)
x_values=seq(0,300, by=10)
y_values=seq(0,50,by=5)
xy_grid=expand.grid(TV=x_values,radio=y_values)
yhat=matrix(predict(sales_lm_int,xy_grid),
         nrow=length(x_values),ncol=length(y_values))
adv_3d=plot_ly(advertising,x=~TV,y=~radio,z=~sales)
adv_3d |> 
  add_markers(marker = list(color = "black", size = 3)) |>
  add_surface(x = ~x_values, 
              y = ~y_values, 
              z = ~t(yhat),
              colorscale = "Viridis",
              opacity = 0.7) |>
  layout(scene = list(
    xaxis = list(title = "TV"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Radio"),
    zaxis = list(title = "Sales")
  ))





Its so beautiful it brings tears to my eyes.
A second way of visualizing the interactive effect of TV and radio is to compare the slopes of the regression lines for sales vs TV when radio is high vs low. First, we need to engineer a new variable to represent the latter splitting which we will base on the median

mr=median(advertising$radio)
advertising$radio_level=ifelse(advertising$radio>mr,"high","low")
advertising |>
  ggplot(aes(x=TV,y=sales,color=radio_level))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",se=FALSE)+
  scale_color_manual(values=c("darkorange","#17806d"))








You can see that unlike in the beerwings example, the slopes of the regression lines are different for the two groups: when radio spending is high, you also get more “bang for your buck” in terms of TV spending too (higher slope). This is the reason an interactive effect is also sometimes called a synergy effect (at least when the coefficient is positive).

title: Module 2.2: Enriching Linear Models
text:
Polynomial Terms
The final type of enrichment we’ll discuss in this section is the addition of polynomial terms in linear models5. To motivate this, lets look at the mtcars dataset which is built into R and has specs on 30 different makes of cars:

You may not know much about cars (I sure don’t!) but if you’re driving one that takes gas, I’m sure you’re paying lots of attention to the mpg column these days. Suppose we want to see how mpg depends on the horsepower (hp) of the car:

mtcars |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=hp,y=mpg))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method=lm,
              color="#D55E00")








This doesn’t look very linear6 even though we get a significant linear coefficient and decent \(R^2\) :

fit_lm=lm(mpg~hp,mtcars)
summary(fit_lm)


Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-5.7121 -2.1122 -0.8854  1.5819  8.2360

Multiple R-squared:  0.6024,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5892 
F-statistic: 45.46 on 1 and 30 DF,  p-value: 1.788e-07

\[
mpg = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (hp) + \beta_2 (hp)^2 + \varepsilon
\]
This requires engineering a new variable \((hp)^2\) which lm will do automatically:

fit_lm_quad=lm(mpg~hp+I(hp^2),mtcars)
summary(fit_lm_quad)

mtcars |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=hp,y=mpg))+

              formula=y~poly(x,2),
              color = "#0072B2")








To get a more realistic model which incorporates curvature without the increase, we need to use a data transformation. This and a few other topics related to regression diagnostics will be discussed in 2.3.

Practice

title: Module 2.2: Enriching Linear Models
text:
Footnotes


Sometimes viewed as a special case of one-hot encoding where one creates a separate column of 0/1s for each possible value of a categorical variable.↩︎
Not to imply that Gender is binary, but there were only two values recorded in this dataset. It was Minnesota in the early 2000s.↩︎
The hypothesis test for nonzero slope is essentially equivalent to doing a two-sample t-test for comparing average beer consumption between genders except that the degrees of freedom is different.↩︎
You can also set up contrasts between categories which allow you to interpret coefficients relative to the overall mean. Look up the documentation of contrasts for details.↩︎
It may seem strange to call polynomial models linear, but as you can see below, they are linear in the coefficients \(\beta_i\). The nonlinearity only creates additional features to engineer.↩︎
We’ll further discuss checking for nonlinearity Module 2.3↩︎

title: Module 2 Bonus: \(F\)-test
text: This section goes deeper into the statistical theory behind model comparison. It is optional but recommended for students with a strong statistics background or those planning to take further courses in statistics or machine learning.

title: Module 2 Bonus: \(F\)-test
text:
Introduction
In these notes, we will be explaining the last line of the regression output
